title: Batching visibility profiling and kernel hotspots - field notes
content:
Purpose:
This note captures a targeted profiling run that tried to increase "visibility" into how batch formation and the runtime dispatch pipeline interact with GPU kernel hotspots. Goal: identify per-request wait time hotspots (where requests spend time before token generation) and kernel-level hotspots during generation that amplify tail latency under mixed loads.

Background and hypothesis:
- We see occasional 99.9th tail spikes for medium-length requests (avg tokens 80-150) while p50/p95 remain fine.
- Hypothesis A: a non-trivial fraction of tail is spent in pre-dispatch (queue + serialization + memcpy) rather than compute.
- Hypothesis B: some model kernels (attention softmax, KV memcpy, layernorm) have large variance and get amplified for certain sequence lengths or microbatch shapes.

Environment and how we measured:
- Cluster: dedicated GPU pool (A100 40GB), CUDA 11.8, PyTorch 2.2 + Triton-backed custom kernels for attention.
- Runtime version: serving-runtime@release-2024-10-10 + lightweight telemetry patch that adds microtrace ids per request.
- Workload: mixed traffic with 60% short (<32 tokens), 30% medium (80 tokens), 10% long (300 tokens). QPS ramped from 50 -> 120 -> 200.
- Tools: nsight compute (kernel timeline, hardware counters), nvprof for memcopy stacks, eBPF uprobe+tracepoints for user-space queue wait times, and our internal microtrace join (frontend queue time, batch formation time, prefill time, dispatch latency, kernel launch latency, kernel compute time, postprocess).

Key instrumentation additions for this run (small dev effort):
1) Per-request microtrace id propagated through queue -> batch formation -> GPU dispatch -> completion.
2) Per-batch summary logged to trace collector: batch_size, composition (how many short/medium/long), earliest_arrival_ts, flush_reason (timeout/size/force), dispatch_ts, gpu_queue_enqueue_ts, first_kernel_launch_ts, last_kernel_end_ts.
3) Kernel annotation layer added to mark logical kernels: ATTENTION_SOFTMAX, KV_COPY, LAYER_NORM, MATMUL_FWD, TOKEN_SCORING.

Summary of observations (high level):
- 60% of 99.9th tail minutes had > 40ms of pre-dispatch wait (time from request arrival to batch dispatch).
- Kernel compute variance: ATTENTION_SOFTMAX and KV_COPY together accounted for ~42% of per-batch compute time variance as sequence length increased.
- Memcopy patterns: many medium-length requests ended up participating in microbatches that forced multiple small cudaMemcpyAsync calls (fragmented transfers) which had higher latency than fewer large transfers.
- Dispatch jitter: when batches contain mixed length sequences, kernel-launch patterns produce serialized kernel execution vs. coalesced fused-kernels, increasing latency for longer sequences in the same batch.

Representative microtrace (timestamps relative to request arrival):
- t0: request arrival
- t0 + 3.2ms: enqueued into per-GPU queue (queue wait due to previous flush)
- t0 + 8.7ms: assigned to batch #2374 (batch size 6; 4 short, 2 medium)
- t0 + 8.9ms: batch formation done, serialized request for prefill
- t0 + 12.1ms: cudaMemcpyAsync for KV_COPY start (small, 96KB)
- t0 + 12.9ms: ATTENTION_SOFTMAX kernel launch (short kernel, high overhead)
- t0 + 26.4ms: token produced (end-to-end for this request: 26.4ms)
Note: in the 99.9th percentiles we observed pre-dispatch steps stretched to 45-120ms depending on backlog and timeout flush policy.

Profiling details and numbers:
1) Pre-dispatch wait distribution (from microtrace collected over 6h):
- p50: 4.1ms, p90: 15.9ms, p95: 27.4ms, p99: 58.2ms, p999: 128.6ms
- Correlation: p99 requests often coincided with flush_reason == timeout and batch composition being mixed.

2) Per-kernel compute time (median across batches of size 8):
- MATMUL_FWD: p50 2.8ms, p95 6.2ms
- ATTENTION_SOFTMAX: p50 1.2ms, p95 4.9ms (high tail)
- KV_COPY (device <-> device staging): p50 0.8ms, p95 3.7ms (high variance due to fragmented memcpy)
- LAYER_NORM: p50 0.3ms, p95 0.9ms

3) Memcopy fragmentation metric (new): number of distinct cudaMemcpyAsync calls per request prefill
- Short requests: avg 1.2 calls/request
- Medium requests: avg 3.9 calls/request
- Long requests: avg 6.1 calls/request
- Impact: requests with >=4 memcpy calls had 2.2x higher memcpy p95 latency than those with <=2 calls.

Root-cause hypotheses derived from data:
A) Timeout flushes interacting with mixed-length coalescing produce batches where long sequences are artificially delayed by waiting for short sequences to serialize prefill or by causing more fragmented memcpy passes.
B) The attention softmax implementation is sensitive to warp launch shapes and shows superlinear latency as sequence length crosses certain thresholds — when those requests are grouped with short sequences (so microbatch shapes vary), the kernel schedule leads to serialized small kernel invocations instead of fewer larger, more efficient launches.
C) The current fairness demotion logic treats sequence length as a soft hint; we need stronger per-request shape-aware routing to avoid head-of-line blocking for medium/long requests.

Experiments run and results (short descriptions):
Experiment 1 - Increase default coalesce timeout from 2ms -> 6ms under low utilization (QPS < 60).
- Result: pre-dispatch p95 reduced from 27.4ms -> 14.1ms, p999 reduced from 128ms -> 76ms. Throughput impact negligible at low utilization.
- Side-effect: slightly higher p50 (1ms) because more requests waited to form larger batches but average token cost per request fell.

Experiment 2 - Batch shape bucketing: ensure batches are composed of similar sequence length buckets (short/medium/long) by adding a quick bucketing step before final coalescing.
- Implementation: per-worker fast histogram with three sliding buckets; flush thresholds vary per bucket (short: size 12 or 10ms timeout; medium: size 8 or 6ms; long: size 4 or 3ms).
- Result: medium request p99 tail reduced by 32%; overall memcopy fragmentation reduced (medium avg 3.9 -> 2.1 calls).

Experiment 3 - Consolidate memcopies: implement a staging buffer aggregation where contiguous small memcopies are concatenated into a single contiguous transfer where possible.
- Result: KV_COPY p95 reduced ~45% for medium/long requests. Additional CPU overhead for building staging buffers observed but under quota.

Experiment 4 - Kernel fusion probe: run an A/B where Triton fused kernels are used for attention+softmax for medium-length shapes.
- Result: for medium-only batches, ATTENTION+SOFTMAX combined showed 30-50% p95 improvement; however, incompatible with batches that mix shapes.

Actionable tuning recommendations (short-term, medium-term):
Short-term (1-2 sprints):
- Raise coalesce timeout adaptively when observed QPS < 70 to allow better batching and reduce pre-dispatch jitter.
- Introduce coarse length-bucketing before batch formation to avoid mixed-shape batches.
- Add memcopy aggregator for small transfers; fallback to previous path if staging would increase CPU time beyond threshold.
- Add microtrace sampling (1% of requests) permanently to detect regressions and verify improvements.

Medium-term (quarter):
- Rework attention softmax kernel to be less shape-sensitive (investigate warp-level reduction strategy, reduce kernel launch overhead by grouping contiguous launches).
- Introduce shape-aware scheduler policy to prefer homogeneous microbatches when contention or tail events are detected.
- Surface batch composition analytics in Console: per-model breakdown of batch shapes, flush reasons, and memcopy call counts.

Risks and trade-offs:
- Increasing timeout improves coalescing but increases p50 for ultra-low latency scenarios. We mitigate by making this adaptive to per-route SLOs.
- Bucketing reduces mixing efficiency (fewer "perfectly-sized" batches) which can increase GPU idle time under some distributions. Need to monitor unit cost per token.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- What is the trade-off curve for bucketing granularity? Two buckets vs three vs continuous bucketing (cost vs tail reduction).
- Is there a way to signal to caller SDK that request will be delayed opportunistically (probabilistic latency hint) to improve batching without surprising users?
- Could we detect when kernel fusion is beneficial at runtime and dynamically switch (cost of JIT/fusion vs stable improvement)?

Next steps (owners assigned):
- Arjun: implement memcopy aggregator RFC + perf test (due 2024-11-15).
- Lina: prototype per-worker bucketing and metric plumbing into trace collector (due 2024-11-12).
- Tom: kernel fusion A/B extension and hardware counter runs to measure warp efficiency (due 2024-11-22).
- Maya: coordinate Console visualization mockups for batch composition metrics (due 2024-11-08).

Appendix (quick commands and probes used):
- microtrace tail fetch: curl -s "https://telemetry.internal/trace/query?model=X&since=6h&sample=1%" | jq '.events | map(select(.phase=="pre_dispatch"))'
- nvprof snapshot: nvprof --profile-child-processes --log-file nvprof.log python -m serving_runtime.bench --profile
- nsight compute: ncu --target-processes all --kernel-id ::ATTENTION_SOFTMAX --export attention.ncu-rep ./serve
- eBPF probe used to capture queue wait: bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:sched:sched_wakeup { @[comm] = count(); }' (adapted to user-space enqueue tracepoint)

Closing note:
This run suggests a large fraction of the worst tail is not pure GPU compute but the interaction between batch formation, memcopy patterns, and kernel launch shapes. Targeted fixes on coalescing heuristics, memcopy aggregation, and shape-aware bucketing produced measurable tail improvements with acceptable trade-offs. The longer-term fix likely involves kernel-level work and dynamic scheduler policies that prefer homogeneous microbatches when tail signals appear.

If you want raw traces or the trace-join script, ping me (maya.chen@redwood.ai) and I will drop the artifacts into the shared drive.
